title: On the pseudorandomness of simple quantum processes
authors: Jesko Dujmovic, Jonas Haferkamp, Alexander Poremba
abstract: Can simple processes appear highly complex? Gowers (Comb. Prob. Comp. '96) conjectured that repeatedly composing local random reversible operations can yield global permutations that are indistinguishable from random. In this work, we study the unitary quantum analog of this question, in an attempt to make new progress on this longstanding conjecture.   Our first result shows that statistical moment matching in the form of unitary designs does not generically lead to pseudorandomness---even for the simplest quantum processes: for every fixed $t$, we give an efficiently samplable family $\{ν_n\}_n$ of distributions on one- and two-qubit gates such that, after $T=O_t(n^2\log^2 n)$ independent steps, the resulting $n$-qubit ensemble is an approximate unitary $t$-design with negligible error $\exp(-Ω(\log^2 n))$, yet an efficient quantum algorithm distinguishes it from random using only $O_t(\log^2 n)$ queries. This refutes the unitary analog of the Hoory--Magen--Myers--Rackoff conjecture (ICALP '04) for permutations.   Our second result is a stronger separation between unitary designs and pseudorandom unitaries at polynomially bounded moments; our counterexample, however, requires highly structured ensembles, in contrast with the simple local walks from before. This suggests caution when using unitary designs to model information scrambling in black-hole physics, as even maximally scrambled systems can exhibit structure which is accessible to efficient experiments. Motivated by these findings, we then propose new conjectures for how pseudorandomness can plausibly emerge within simple quantum processes, such as random quantum circuits.
summary: This paper explores the gap between statistical randomness and computational randomness in quantum circuits. The authors prove that even if a quantum process matches the statistical moments of a truly random unitary (a $t$-design), it can still be distinguished from random by a quantum computer. This suggests that achieving pseudorandomness requires more than just matching low-order moments.
main_problem: The paper investigates the quantum analog of the Gowers conjecture: whether simple, local random quantum processes can generate unitaries indistinguishable from truly random ones.
main_result: The authors refute the unitary analog of the Hoory–Magen–Myers–Rackoff conjecture, showing that achieving strong statistical moment matching (unitary $t$-designs) does not guarantee computational pseudorandomness.
method: The work involves constructing explicit counterexamples by comparing statistical measures (unitary $t$-designs) against computational indistinguishability using efficient quantum distinguishing algorithms.
model_or_system: The model involves random quantum circuits formed by composing local quantum gates (e.g., two-qubit gates sampled from the Haar measure) acting on $n$ qubits.
key_observables: Unitary $t$-design properties (matching unitary moments) and the ability of an efficient quantum algorithm to distinguish the ensemble from the Haar measure.
important_parameters: The depth of the circuit ($T = O(n^2 \log^2 n)$) and the order of the moment ($t$).
main_assumptions: The analysis compares the ensemble to the Haar measure and relies on the existence of efficient quantum distinguishing algorithms.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates a classical random reversible circuit, and Figure 2 shows a simple nearest-neighbor random quantum circuit using two-qubit gates.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first showing a refutation of the unitary analog of the HMMR conjecture using simple local walks, followed by a stronger separation result requiring highly structured ensembles, and concluding with new conjectures for pseudorandomness.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous theoretical boundary, showing that simple structural properties (like moment matching) are insufficient guarantees for true quantum randomness, which is crucial for understanding quantum scrambling in physics.
